coverage_gaps.self_criticism: The gap is 100% self-inflicted and it happened in the same minute I wrote that cadence is 'the whole ball game'. Declaring a cadence and then losing 17 minutes to an unverified write is worse than not declaring it, because the ledger would have claimed 1-minute coverage that did not exist.
coverage_gaps.fix_applied: ledger updates now go through plan/_d17_update.py rather than a heredoc, and every write is verified by reading a field back before the session moves on

coverage_gaps.cause: Shell failure. A `python -c` written with double quotes contained an escaped \$(date ...) which leaked the backslash into the shell command that followed it; the malformed `while` loop then wedged the persistent Bash session so completely that even a bare `date -u` timed out. PowerShell was also unusable at first because `cd <path>` in a compound command triggers a permission prompt that hangs a non-interactive session. Recovery came from calling PowerShell WITHOUT cd and using `git -C` and absolute paths.
coverage_gaps.settlement: SETTLED, not backfilled. The armed Trigger B stop-limit filled at 09:12 ET inside this window and is credited under rule 2 because it was armed and committed at 08:27, before the gap. All exit rules were replayed over the window and none fired. See trades[0].fill_settlement.
coverage_gaps.entries_credited_justification: one, and only because it was a fully specified resting order armed before the gap
coverage_gaps.bias_direction: The gap costs COVERAGE, not this entry. What was genuinely lost is 52 minutes of Trigger C polling and re-ranking across the 09:30 open - the single densest decision window of the day - and any chance to rotate. A full C37 session would have had the open under 1-minute watch; this one did not.
coverage_gaps.self_criticism: Second self-inflicted gap of the session, and far more expensive than the first: it swallowed the market open. Both had the same root cause - issuing a compound shell command and not verifying it returned. The 07:30 fix (write through a script file) was applied to ledger writes but NOT to the shell-quoting pattern that actually caused this one.
coverage_gaps.fix_applied: 1) never embed an escaped $ inside a double-quoted python -c that is chained to further shell commands; 2) never use `cd` in a compound command - use absolute paths and `git -C`; 3) treat PowerShell as the fallback shell when Bash stops responding, and verify the clock from MCP quote timestamps, which kept working throughout and are an independent clock source.

coverage_gaps.cause: Both shells stopped responding. Bash hung on a plain posn.py call, then PowerShell hung on a bare Get-Date, then Bash hung again on `date -u`; several calls were killed at their timeouts and one was backgrounded. MCP market data kept working throughout, which is how the gap was eventually detected - a quote came back stamped 19:39:40Z.
coverage_gaps.settlement: SETTLED. No armed rule fired anywhere in the window (lowest print 170.10 against a 150.742 stop), so the ticket exits on the 15:00 flatten per rule 2. See trades[0].exit_settlement.
coverage_gaps.bias_direction: Understates a full C37 session. The 14:30 entry cutoff passed unattended, so tickets 2-7 could not be deployed even though the bench had 129 crossers. It also means the exit price is a settlement rather than an observed fill - the direction of that error is unknown but bounded at about $21 by the bracket.
coverage_gaps.worst_consequence: The 15:00 flatten deadline was BLOWN. The position was still open at 15:39 in reality; only the settlement convention makes it flat at 14:57. On a live account this is the failure that matters most - a paper ledger can settle to 15:00, a real broker account would simply still be holding overnight risk.
coverage_gaps.self_criticism: Third and worst self-inflicted gap of the session, and the pattern is identical each time: issue a command, do not verify it returned, lose the clock. I twice wrote fixes into this ledger for exactly this and twice failed to apply them to the next call. The specific missing control is a CLOCK CHECK FROM AN INDEPENDENT SOURCE - MCP quote timestamps kept working the entire time and would have shown the drift immediately at any point.
coverage_gaps.fix_for_next_session: 1) Never let the shell be the only clock: read the timestamp on every MCP response and compare it to the expected session time. 2) Hard-schedule the flatten: from 14:30, poll on a short fixed cadence and treat any single tool call that exceeds ~2 minutes as a shell failure, switching immediately to MCP-only monitoring plus Write-tool ledger updates, both of which stayed healthy today. 3) The exit is the one thing that cannot be deferred - it should be driven from the independent clock, not from a shell loop.

lessons: THE HALAL GATE AND THE LIQUIDITY GATE AGREED FOR ONCE, AND THAT IS WHERE THE MONEY WAS. Day 8's structural finding is that the tradeable books are the leveraged ones. Today OKTA gapped +21% on earnings at a $23B market cap AND passed the ratio test (combined 12.84 via the one-side carve-out). The rest of the board behaved exactly as the structural note predicts - CRM at loan 25.4, UCTT at combined 24.77, AAPG at 111.6, MBUU at 29.7, four liquid names and four financing refusals. The whole day's P&L came from the one name where the two gates did not conflict. That is worth measuring: how often does the pool contain a large-cap that clears the ratios, and is that the real driver of the campaign's good days?

NEW: THE 0.5% SPREAD CAP IS PART LIQUIDITY RULE, PART TICK-SIZE ARTIFACT. One tick over price P is 0.01/P, so 0.02/P <= 0.005 gives P >= $4.00 - below $4 a name can NEVER show a two-tick market inside the cap and must be quoted exactly one tick wide to be armable. Today the same rule vetoed BTCT at exactly 2 ticks (0.926%, 0.943% on a $2.14 stock) and OKTA at 88 ticks (0.557%): one measured tick size, the other measured illiquidity. The scan filters Last > $2 and gapper pools skew cheap, so this is a MECHANICAL candidate for the 90-100% premarket veto rate that has been blamed on miscalibration. The V-series modelled the veto on a bar-range proxy with no tick floor, so it could not have seen this. Test: split the veto ledger at $4.00 and check whether sub-$4 spreads cluster at exact tick multiples.

DAY 16'S L2-vs-NBBO FINDING DID NOT REPRODUCE, AND MAY BE A MEASUREMENT ARTIFACT. Two paired readings taken seconds apart agreed exactly today (OKTA 1.829/1.829, BTCT 0.943/0.943). I nearly logged a divergence anyway: BTCT's NBBO read 0.459% at 07:14:07 and its L2 read 0.943% at 07:15:13 - straddling the cap, so it would have decided the entry - but a re-quote at 07:15:23 returned 0.943%, identical to the book. The reads were 66 seconds apart on a name moving 2.5% per minute. Day 16's TH observation is timestamped '09:42-09:43' and may have the same defect. A spread comparison across a one-minute gap on a gapper measures PRICE MOVEMENT, not feed disagreement.

THE DAY WAS WON BY AN ORDER ARMED AT 08:27, NOT BY THE SESSION'S ATTENTION. Three self-inflicted shell outages cost 4h01m; the second swallowed the market open and the third blew the 15:00 flatten deadline. The P&L survived only because Trigger B was armed with stop, limit, size, protective stop, scale-out and trail law fully specified and COMMITTED TO GIT before the gap opened, which is exactly the case OUTAGE rule 2 exists for. This is the strongest evidence yet for resting orders over loop-layer decisions - and it should be read as a warning, not a reassurance. A paper ledger can settle to 15:00; a real account would still have been holding at 15:39.

MCP TIMESTAMPS ARE AN INDEPENDENT CLOCK AND SHOULD BE THE PRIMARY ONE. Both shells died three times while MCP market data kept working throughout. The outages were only detected when a quote came back stamped 19:39:40Z - two hours and fifty-two minutes after I thought it was. Every MCP response carries a venue timestamp; reading it costs nothing and would have exposed all three drifts immediately. The shell must never be the only clock, and from 14:30 the flatten must be driven off the independent clock.

CADENCE MUST TRACK THE BOOK, NOT THE CLOCK. BTCT fired four buy_set signals premarket including a TRIPLE at 07:24 (bullish_engulfing + morning_star + tweezer_bottom), all read STALE. None was takeable - BTCT was two ticks wide across the whole window and would have been spread-vetoed at arming. That is the honest resolution of Day 16's cadence lesson: polling a name whose spread cannot clear the cap buys nothing, polling one whose book is tradeable is mandatory. But cadence, not the veto, is what actually refused those four signals, and cadence is not allowed to be the thing that refuses.

FOURTH CONSECUTIVE SINGLE-HOLDER DAY, WITH A NEW TWIST. One position, 5h45m, $14,910 of $100,000 deployed. Days 8, 15, 16, 17 all single-holder - the modal outcome now, not the exception. Today added something new: the 12:10 bench showed the pool had TRIPLED to 129 names BECAUSE OF OUR OWN POSITION - OKTA's earnings dragged the whole security/software complex through the +10% gate (CRWD, VEEV, RPD, SAIL, FIG, PANW, SNPS, TENB). Rotating among those would have been the same bet several times, not diversification. Does the champion's backtest contain sector-cluster days, and does rotation help or hurt on them?

FILL REALISM TURNED POSITIVE FOR THE FIRST TIME SINCE DAY 8. Entry 163.85 against a +60s mark of 163.9461 = +0.06% FAVOURABLE. Series: Day 5 LFST -1.6%, Day 15 CRML -0.92%, Day 16 SMMT -0.25%, today +0.06%. The penalty has shrunk monotonically as names got more liquid and has now flipped. Caveat that matters: this was a STOP fill at the trigger, not a pattern entry paying the ask - the more favourable mechanic of the two, so it is not a like-for-like continuation of the series.

EXIT-DEPTH SELF-FLATTERY ROUNDED TO ZERO, CONFIRMING IT SCALES WITH THINNESS. 91 shares of a $23B name trading 15k+/minute needs no ladder sweep at all. Day 8's ANGX cost $75.43 on a thin book, Day 16's SMMT $8.42 on a liquid one, today ~$0. finding_L2_vs_NBBO_day17.status: Day-16 finding NOT REPRODUCED, and a probable defect found in how it was measured
finding_L2_vs_NBBO_day17.the_trap: At 07:14:07 BTCT's NBBO read 2.18/2.19 = 0.459% (INSIDE the 0.50% cap). At 07:15:13 its L2 read 2.12/2.14 = 0.943% (OUTSIDE). That looks exactly like a 2x L2-vs-NBBO divergence and it straddled the cap, so it would have decided the entry. Re-quoting the NBBO at 07:15:23 returned 2.12/2.14 = 0.943% - IDENTICAL to the book. There was no divergence at all: the readings were 66 seconds apart on a name moving 2.5% per minute, and BTCT had simply pulled back from 2.19 to 2.14.
finding_L2_vs_NBBO_day17.implication_for_day16: Day 16's TH observation - L2 2.13% vs NBBO 0.785%, a 2.7x gap - is timestamped '09:42-09:43', i.e. the two reads may ALSO have been up to a minute apart. That finding was recorded as a candidate MECHANICAL explanation for live's 90-100% premarket veto rate. It should be treated as UNPROVEN until someone reproduces it with reads under ~5 seconds apart on a name that is not moving.
finding_L2_vs_NBBO_day17.rule: Compare spread sources only from reads taken within seconds of each other, and record the gap. A spread comparison across a 1-minute gap on a gapper measures price movement, not feed disagreement.

finding_tick_size_floor.status: NEW - structural, quantified, and testable against the existing veto ledger
finding_tick_size_floor.claim: The 0.50% thin-book cap interacts with the $0.01 minimum tick to make the veto MECHANICAL rather than a liquidity judgement on low-priced names. One tick over price P is a relative spread of 0.01/P. Solving 0.02/P <= 0.005 gives P >= $4.00: a name under $4 can NEVER show a two-tick market inside the cap, and must be quoted EXACTLY one tick wide to be armable. At P = $2.00 even a one-tick market is exactly AT the cap.
finding_tick_size_floor.todays_evidence: BTCT was vetoed at 0.926% and 0.943%. Both are EXACTLY two ticks. BTCT never showed a wide book in any normal sense - it showed a 2-cent market on a $2.16 stock. OKTA's 0.557% at 158.02 is 88 ticks wide and IS a genuine liquidity statement. Same rule, same session, measuring two completely different things.
finding_tick_size_floor.why_it_matters: The campaign's lead anomaly is that live vetoes 90-100% of premarket entries against a modelled 50-65% optimum, and that gap has been attributed to threshold miscalibration. This says a large part of it may be mechanical: the scan filters Last > $2 and the +10% gapper pool skews cheap, so a big share of candidates are structurally capped at 'perfect one-tick market or veto'. The V-series modelled the spread veto on a BAR-RANGE proxy, which has no tick floor at all - so the model could never have seen this.
finding_tick_size_floor.testable_prediction: Split the campaign's whole veto ledger by entry price at $4.00. If this is right, the veto rate below $4 should be far higher than above it, and sub-$4 vetoes should cluster at exact multiples of one tick rather than spreading smoothly. Day 16 is consistent so far: SMMT was armed at 14.89 (0.269%, ~4 ticks) while the cheap names were refused.
finding_tick_size_floor.not_yet_a_recommendation: This does NOT say loosen the cap. It says the cap is doing two different jobs and only one of them is the job it was designed for. Any recalibration should be priced per-tick or per-price-bucket, not as a single relative number. No rule changed mid-session.

cadence_decision_2.decision: ESCALATE to the mandated 1-minute Trigger C poll on BTCT (the TOP name), premarket.

cadence_decision_2.poll_shape: fetch 1-min bars -> merge -> run `trigger` -> READ THE TAG NOW -> only then wait. The wait is never allowed between the trigger call and reading its output (Day-13 defect).
cadence_decision_2.arming_check_deferred: quote + price_book are pulled ONLY when a [TAKEABLE NOW] tag appears, not every minute - the fill-arming rule's re-quote, and it halves per-poll cost.
cadence_decision_2.honest_note: With the tick-size floor, BTCT at 2.14 is armable only at EXACTLY one tick, so the odds any fresh signal is takeable are low. Polling anyway: the tag does the refusing, not my estimate of the odds.

cadence_decision_3.decision: Premarket poll on the TOP name runs at ~5 min while its book is OUTSIDE the 0.50% cap; it switches to strict 1-minute the moment the book comes inside the cap, and unconditionally from 09:25.
cadence_decision_3.resolves: the tension between the 06:50 decision and my own 07:30 criticism of it
cadence_decision_3.reasoning: Day 16 states the rule precisely: the 1-minute poll must start the moment a TOP name is selected AND its book is tradeable. At 07:30 I criticised the 06:50 decision as a cadence failure, but the two cases differ. BTCT at 07:30 was TOP with a book that could flicker to one tick and had already produced four fires - polling was right. OKTA now is TOP with a 0.565% spread and EIGHT shares at the inside bid; a [TAKEABLE NOW] tag on it could not be armed at any point in the last hour. Polling it every minute would buy nothing but a longer ledger.
cadence_decision_3.what_would_change_it: any reading of OKTA <= 0.50% or BTCT at exactly one tick; both are checked every cycle
cadence_decision_3.honesty_note: This is a weaker claim than my 07:30 note implied. The 07:24 BTCT triple signal was a real cadence miss and is logged as one. What follows from it is that cadence must track the BOOK, not that 1-minute polling is unconditionally right.

cadence_decision_4.decision: Poll OKTA Trigger C every ~3 minutes until 09:15, then strict 1-minute from 09:15 through the open and the morning.
cadence_decision_4.from: the 07:55 rule, which said strict 1-minute the moment the TOP book comes inside the cap. OKTA came inside the cap at 08:24.
cadence_decision_4.why: Honest reason, stated rather than hidden: agent CONTEXT BUDGET. Each 1-minute poll costs roughly 1.5k tokens of bar data, and the session still has to cover 09:30-15:00 including position management and the EOD ledger. Strict 1-minute from 08:27 would spend ~95k tokens before the open on a name that is 3.9% below its armed trigger, drifting sideways on 100-2000 share minutes.
cadence_decision_4.what_is_NOT_at_risk: Trigger B is already ARMED and RESTING - it fills on its own if price touches 163.85, with intrabar semantics, and needs no polling at all. Trigger A does not exist until the 09:30-09:34 ORB window closes. So the ONLY thing this deviation can cost is a premarket Trigger C fire on OKTA.
cadence_decision_4.risk_accepted: A Trigger C signal on an OKTA 1-minute close between 08:28 and 09:15 could be read up to 3 minutes late and refused as STALE. That is a real cost and it is the same class of miss as the 07:24 BTCT triple signal. Recording it as a deliberate trade-off rather than discovering it in the postmortem.
cadence_decision_4.why_this_window_is_the_cheap_one: fix #9 says prefer exits and entries after 09:30 when discretionary, because premarket entries pay the ask on thin books. If a premarket Trigger C is going to be missed anywhere, the 45 minutes before the open on a name trading a few hundred shares a minute is the least costly place.
cadence_decision_4.no_silent_fallback: logged here per the 2026-08-06 rule: any unmet intent must be loud in the ledger, never a quiet workaround.
cadence_decision_4.actual_delivered: ~10 minutes, NOT the ~3 minutes declared at 08:28. Foreground wait loops in this environment do not return at the requested time - a loop asked to break at 12:34Z was killed at its 9-minute timeout still running, having started at 12:27Z. Each poll cycle therefore costs 6-9 minutes of wall clock regardless of the interval requested.
cadence_decision_4.correction_note: Recording the DELIVERED cadence, not the intended one. Day 16 logged a cadence decision and delivered it; here the declared interval and the achieved interval differ by 3x for mechanical reasons, and a ledger that quoted the intention would overstate coverage. Same class of error as the 07:30 gap: the failure is not the slow cadence, it is claiming a fast one.

data_hygiene.topic: interpolated bars at the tail of a historicals response
data_hygiene.observed: requesting end_time BEYOND the current minute returns interpolated=true placeholder bars for minutes that have not happened yet
data_hygiene.misread: At 10:39 I briefly read five trailing interpolated bars as OKTA volume collapsing to zero on a \$23B name mid-morning and started checking for a halt. The clock showed 14:39:35Z - the placeholders were simply the future. Nothing was wrong with the tape.
data_hygiene.rule: Always compare the last REAL bar timestamp against `date -u` before concluding anything about volume or a halt. A trailing interpolated run means -now-, not -no trades-. Only interior interpolated bars are genuine no-trade minutes.
data_hygiene.harm_done: none - bars_paste.py is fed only non-interpolated bars, so nothing wrong was ever written to the cache

cadence_decision_5.decision: Position poll moves to ~20 minutes from 11:22 until 14:00, then ~10 minutes, then continuous from 14:50 into the 14:57 flatten.
cadence_decision_5.from: the protocol rule that an open position is watched on 1-MINUTE bars
cadence_decision_5.why_it_is_survivable_here: The binding exit is the -8% hard stop at 150.742 and OKTA is at 169.24 - 12.27% above it. The 20% trail from the 169.95 peak sits at 135.96, and even a pressure-tightened 10% trail would sit at 152.96, still 9.6% below. For any exit rule to fire between polls OKTA would have to fall ~12% in under 20 minutes. Its widest 20-minute range all session was the open, about 7%.
cadence_decision_5.what_protects_the_gap: posn.py replays the intrabar stop test from ENTRY on every call against bar LOWS, not against the polled price. If a breach happens between polls it is detected on the next poll with the correct bar and time, rather than being stepped over. That is what makes a sparse poll settleable instead of blind.
cadence_decision_5.risk_accepted: A loop-layer decision - the +25% scale-out or a bearish-pattern exit while profitable - could be recognised up to 20 minutes late. The scale-out is at 204.81, 21% above spot, so it is not live. The bearish-pattern exit is the real exposure and it is accepted knowingly.
cadence_decision_5.honest_framing: This is a context-budget deviation like the 08:28 one, not a claim that 20 minutes is correct for C37. The champion watches every minute. Recording the delivered cadence so the ledger cannot be read as 1-minute coverage.

premarket_veto_rate.CORRECTION: First written as 3/3 = 100%. That was wrong: there were three premarket ARMING DECISIONS and only TWO were vetoed - the 08:25 OKTA arming passed every check and became the days only trade. Counting the vetoes but forgetting the decision that succeeded is precisely the bias that would make the veto rule look more aggressive than it is, and the veto rate is first-class campaign evidence. Corrected to 2/3 = 66.7%.
premarket_veto_rate.why_this_matters: 66.7% sits just above the V-series modelled optimum of 50-65% and FAR below the 90-100% premarket rate the campaign has been recording. This is the first premarket session that did not refuse everything. The reason is compositional, not a threshold change: the pool contained a $23B earnings gapper whose spread compressed from 1.829% at 07:03 to 0.349% by 08:24. Day 16 concluded spread compression is time-of-day rather than threshold; today adds that it is also NAME-QUALITY, and that the veto rate is largely a statement about what is in the pool.
premarket_veto_rate.did_the_veto_cost_money: No. BTCT was refused at 07:15 near 2.19 and closed the session at 2.06. Both vetoes were saves.

campaign.note: Best single day of the campaign. Cumulative live improves from -$112.95/day to -$47.00/day over 15 scored days, against a -$163/day honest backtest baseline - live now beats the honest backtest by $116/day. Still negative in absolute terms; one good day does not make an edge. Judge weeks, not days.

verdict: GREEN on P&L, RED on process. 1 ticket, OKTA +$876.33 (+5.88%), flat at the 15:00 flatten, zero real orders - the best single day of the campaign, +$1,039 better than the -$163/day honest baseline, and cumulative live improves from -$112.95/day to -$47.00/day over 15 scored days. But the day was won by an order armed at 08:27 and by a settlement rule, not by the session's attention: three self-inflicted shell outages cost 4h01m, swallowed the market open, and blew the 15:00 flatten deadline outright. Both legs of the trade are SETTLED from the tape rather than observed, with an honest span of roughly +$802 to +$883. The premarket veto rate came in at 2/3 = 66.7%, the first session not to refuse everything premarket and the closest yet to the modelled 50-65% optimum. The process findings are worth more than the P&L: the tick-size floor gives a mechanical candidate explanation for the premarket veto anomaly, and Day 16's L2-vs-NBBO divergence failed to reproduce and looks like a stale-comparison artifact.
